change.summary: waitForHealth now awaits a bounded probeHealth(): one fetch per poll, raced against a deadline timer derived from the supervisor deadline AND given an AbortController signal, with the timer cleared and the controller aborted in a finally block and an unread response body cancelled. A redundant post-deadline 50ms sleep is skipped so the timeout error is thrown as soon as the bound expires. Public ProcessSupervisor API and StartVendorOptions are unchanged; no options added.

measuredBound.method: Inline node --input-type=module script (no repo files written) using the real ProcessSupervisor, a real node:net peer that accepts and never writes a response, and a real child process (process.execPath -e setInterval). The child is terminated ~400 ms before the deadline (same measurement window as test 1) so that pre-existing Windows force-stop teardown is excluded from the number.
measuredBound.interpretation: Against a peer that accepts the TCP connection and never responds, waitForHealth rejects with the existing timeout message 28-117 ms after the startup deadline (and 38 ms after a 3000 ms deadline), inside the required ~250 ms of slack. The end-to-end startVendor rejection without terminating the child additionally contains pre-existing Windows force-stop teardown (taskkill /T /F plus the child exit event; ~1-1.5 s on this machine, more under parallel test-file load), which is outside this change.

excludedTeardownObserved.note: Measured during development, no dedicated log: the same test with the force-stop teardown inside the measured window produced elapsedMs=2363 against the mandated 2300 ms bound once the whole suite ran (parallel test files) - it is pre-existing teardown variance, not the health wait.

testDesignDecisions: Both timeout tests use a real node:net server that accepts and never writes a response (no vi.mock, no monkeypatched global fetch) plus a real child process (process.execPath, args ['-e','setInterval(()=>{},1000)']).

A 15000 ms test-level guard races startVendor so a regression is reported as a readable assertion instead of a hung test file; the start promise carries its own rejection handler so teardown cannot cause an unhandled rejection.

Test 1 terminates the supervised child with process.kill(pid,'SIGKILL') ~400 ms before the deadline: the pre-existing Windows force-stop teardown (taskkill /T /F, ~1-1.5 s under load) is thereby outside the measured window and the mandated assertion (elapsed < startupTimeoutMs + 1500 ms) measures the health wait. Without this, the mandated bound was exceeded once by teardown alone under parallel suite load.

Test 3 keeps the untouched timeout path (no child termination) and additionally asserts that shutdown() completes and that no health request is issued after the timeout; it allows at most one dataless teardown socket, because an aborted fetch in Node 24.11/undici opens exactly one such socket, delayed until the blocking taskkill returns.
Cleanup runs in afterEach: peers release/destroy their sockets and close their servers, supervisors shut down, and temp state roots are removed with retries.
limitations: Scope: this bounds waitForHealth only. It claims nothing about R22 beyond that bounding contract and nothing about backend/B0-B10 or the rest of the Effect/Foldkit migration.

Measured end-to-end rejection (startVendor) still includes pre-existing Windows child force-stop teardown (~1-1.5 s), which is unchanged by this slice and is why test 1 removes the child before the deadline for its timing assertion. The teardown path itself is still exercised by test 3 and by the pre-existing suite.
Platform coverage: Windows only in this worktree. The POSIX branch of requestGracefulStop/requestForceStop (SIGTERM/SIGKILL) was not exercised.
The test file is not typechecked by tsc because the package tsconfig excludes test/**/*.ts; it is only transpiled by vitest/esbuild.

Node 24.11/undici behavior measured, not assumed: aborting a fetch opens exactly one additional dataless TCP socket on teardown, deferred by the blocking taskkill. Test 3 treats 'polling' as 'an HTTP request line was written' (load-bearing assertion) and allows at most one teardown-artifact connection in the settled count. A future fetch implementation that opens more than one such socket would need the test revisited.

Behavioral nuance: if the child exits while a hanging probe is in flight, the bounded loop now reports the startup-timeout error at the deadline instead of never returning; with any peer that answers (ok or non-ok) the child-exit check still runs at the top of the next iteration and reports 'exited before becoming healthy'. All other semantics (no healthCheckUrl => healthy immediately, non-ok => keep polling, ok => healthy with exitCode undefined, startupPending/stop-deferral) are unchanged and covered by the existing suite plus the new regression test.
